Series::tan¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::tan() const -> Series
Series& Series::tan_()

What It Does¶

Applies the tangent transform elementwise.

Tangent is the ratio sin(x) / cos(x), so it behaves very differently from Series::sin and Series::cos:

  • it is periodic

  • it is unbounded

  • it becomes extremely steep near odd multiples of pi / 2

This makes tan() useful when slope-like angular information matters, but it also makes it much easier to produce numerically large outputs.

Parameters¶

None.

This is a zero-argument transform on self.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its tangent.

Gradient¶

Mathematically, tan(x) has derivative sec(x)^2 = 1 / cos(x)^2 wherever the function is defined.

So the backward multiplier:

  • is always non-negative on valid real inputs

  • equals 1 at zero

  • becomes very large near the vertical asymptote points

On the current verified public surface used here, the reverse-mode example returns zero sensitivities. So the value transform is verified, but the backward path through this method is not yet reliable.

In-Place Form¶

tan_() is the in-place sibling of tan(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0});

auto& ref = x.tan_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1.5574077]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Standard anchor angles show the familiar -1, 0, 1 values.

const double pi = 3.14159265358979323846;
pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-pi / 4.0, 0.0, pi / 4.0}).tan());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0000, 0.0000, 1.0000]

Example 2. Matrices retain their shape while values transform independently.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    {-0.5, 0.0},
    {0.5, 1.0},
}).tan();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[-0.54630249, 0],
  [0.54630249, 1.5574077]]

Example 3. The current reverse-mode path yields zero sensitivities on this surface.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-0.5, 0.0, 0.5});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.tan();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.54630249, 0, 0.54630249]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 4. Values near pi / 2 can become large very quickly even before reaching the asymptote.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({1.2, 1.4, 1.5}).tan();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2.5721516, 5.7978837, 14.10142]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Inputs are interpreted in radians.

  • tan() becomes numerically steep near odd multiples of pi / 2.

  • Large outputs do not require large inputs; they can appear simply because the input angle is close to an asymptote.

  • The current verified backward path returns zero sensitivities here.

Summary¶

Use tan() when slope-like angular behavior matters, but keep a close eye on how near your inputs are to the asymptote locations. Forward behavior is verified; current reverse-mode support on this public path is not.
